Authorities

Revenue Ruling 59-60

Rev. Rul. 59-60, 1959-1 C.B. 237

Court
Internal Revenue Service

When market quotations are unavailable, the fair market value of closely held stock is determined from all available financial data and all relevant factors under the hypothetical willing-buyer and willing-seller standard; no single formula controls.

Read the opinion

Retrieved from Internal Revenue Service (ruling reproduced in Appendix A) on August 7, 2026. Original source.

Revenue Ruling 59-60 supplies the federal tax framework for valuing closely held stock when no active market quotation exists. Fair market value is the price at which property would change hands between a hypothetical willing buyer and willing seller, neither under compulsion and both reasonably informed. The inquiry considers the nature and history of the business, economic and industry outlook, book value, earning capacity, dividend capacity, goodwill and other intangibles, prior stock sales, and comparable-company market data.

The ruling cautions against mechanical formulas and requires judgment based on the facts. Its hypothetical-buyer premise is a fair-market-value concept, not a definition of statutory fair value in an appraisal or oppression remedy. It therefore provides useful valuation vocabulary but does not itself decide whether a particular state’s fair-value statute includes buyer-specific synergies or shareholder-level discounts.
